sentences.text: Tessa's mortgage fallback costs $120 a month.
sentences.spoken: Tessa's mortgage fallback costs one hundred twenty dollars a month.

sentences.text: She's borrowing $320,000, and in her city that payment is her biggest bill.
sentences.spoken: She's borrowing three hundred twenty thousand dollars, and in her city that payment is her biggest bill.

sentences.text: [curious] A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year paid off in 15 years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month?
sentences.spoken: [curious] A fifteen-year mortgage, or a thirty-year paid off in fifteen years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month?

sentences.text: We replayed every week of US mortgage surveys to price that fallback in dollars, and what each extra dollar of principal earns.
sentences.spoken: We replayed every week of U.S. mortgage surveys to price that fallback in dollars, and what each extra dollar of principal earns.

sentences.text: Tessa is illustrative, but her rates are real: the survey for the week of October eighth, 2026 has the 15-year at 6.73 percent and the 30-year at 7.4 percent.
sentences.spoken: Tessa is illustrative, but her rates are real: the survey for the week of October eighth, twenty twenty-six has the fifteen-year at six point seven three percent and the thirty-year at seven point four percent.

sentences.text: This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast.
sentences.spoken: This is U.S. only, and it's history, not a forecast.

sentences.text: It won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest.
sentences.spoken: It won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest.

sentences.text: Here is what Tessa is weighing.
sentences.spoken: Here is what Tessa is weighing.

sentences.text: On $320,000, the 15-year loan's payment is $2,828 a month.
sentences.spoken: On three hundred twenty thousand dollars, the fifteen-year loan's payment is two thousand eight hundred twenty-eight dollars a month.

sentences.text: The 30-year loan only requires $2,216.
sentences.spoken: The thirty-year loan only requires two thousand two hundred sixteen dollars.

sentences.text: That gap, about $613 a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the 30-year asks of her.
sentences.spoken: That gap, about six hundred thirteen dollars a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the thirty-year asks of her.

sentences.text: The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a big repair could squeeze it.
sentences.spoken: The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a big repair could squeeze it.

sentences.text: Still, she wants the house paid off in 15 years, so the 30-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan.
sentences.spoken: Still, she wants the house paid off in fifteen years, so the thirty-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan.

sentences.text: At 7.4 percent, finishing that loan in 15 years takes $2,948 a month.
sentences.spoken: At seven point four percent, finishing that loan in fifteen years takes two thousand nine hundred forty-eight dollars a month.

sentences.text: That's $120 a month more than the 15-year loan, for the same house and the same 15 years.
sentences.spoken: That's one hundred twenty dollars a month more than the fifteen-year loan, for the same house and the same fifteen years.

sentences.text: Over those 15 years, the extra adds up to $21,622.
sentences.spoken: Over those fifteen years, the extra adds up to twenty-one thousand six hundred twenty-two dollars.

sentences.text: In Tessa's world, that price is a stack of bills beside her house: the stack is what keeping the fallback costs.
sentences.spoken: In Tessa's world, that price is a stack of bills beside her house: the stack is what keeping the fallback costs.

sentences.text: It exists because the 30-year carries a higher rate on the same balance: on October eighth, 0.67 point higher.
sentences.spoken: It exists because the thirty-year carries a higher rate on the same balance: on October eighth, zero point six seven point higher.

sentences.text: Paid on its own 30-year schedule, her loan would charge $477,622 in interest.
sentences.spoken: Paid on its own thirty-year schedule, her loan would charge four hundred seventy-seven thousand six hundred twenty-two dollars in interest.

sentences.text: Paid in 15 years, it charges $210,691.
sentences.spoken: Paid in fifteen years, it charges two hundred ten thousand six hundred ninety-one dollars.

sentences.text: The 15-year loan charges $189,069, and the difference between those last two totals is exactly the stack.
sentences.spoken: The fifteen-year loan charges one hundred eighty-nine thousand sixty-nine dollars, and the difference between those last two totals is exactly the stack.

sentences.text: So the 30-year paid in 15 isn't the same loan as the 15-year: it's the 15-year plus a fallback, and the fallback has a price.
sentences.spoken: So the thirty-year paid in fifteen isn't the same loan as the fifteen-year: it's the fifteen-year plus a fallback, and the fallback has a price.

sentences.text: Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is the week of October eighth unusual?
sentences.spoken: Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is the week of October eighth unusual?

sentences.text: Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win.
sentences.spoken: Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win.

sentences.text: Here, a real 15-year loan stands next to the 30-year paid in 15, at the real rates of every week since 1991.
sentences.spoken: Here, a real fifteen-year loan stands next to the thirty-year paid in fifteen, at the real rates of every week since nineteen ninety-one.

sentences.text: We priced the same $320,000 both ways in each of 1,833 weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description.
sentences.spoken: We priced the same three hundred twenty thousand dollars both ways in each of one thousand eight hundred thirty-three weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description.

sentences.text: Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question: what would the fallback have cost then?
sentences.spoken: Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question: what would the fallback have cost then?

sentences.text: The answer comes down to one thing: how far the 30-year rate sits above the 15-year.
sentences.spoken: The answer comes down to one thing: how far the thirty-year rate sits above the fifteen-year.

sentences.text: Since 1991, that gap has run from 0.2 point to 1.0 point.
sentences.spoken: Since nineteen ninety-one, that gap has run from zero point two point to one point zero point.

sentences.text: It averaged 0.57 point, and was at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks.
sentences.spoken: It averaged zero point five seven point, and was at least half a point in about two in three weeks.

sentences.text: Tessa's gap on October eighth sits a little above that average.
sentences.spoken: Tessa's gap on October eighth sits a little above that average.

sentences.text: Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap.
sentences.spoken: Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap.

sentences.text: The smallest was $6,097.
sentences.spoken: The smallest was six thousand ninety-seven dollars.

sentences.text: The tallest was $29,502.
sentences.spoken: The tallest was twenty-nine thousand five hundred two dollars.

sentences.text: The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at $16,631.
sentences.spoken: The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at sixteen thousand six hundred thirty-one dollars.

sentences.text: [serious] Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it.
sentences.spoken: [serious] Fewer than one in five weeks since nineteen ninety-one put a price this high on it.

sentences.text: That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history.
sentences.spoken: That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history.

sentences.text: What a lower payment is worth in a bad month, this replay can't measure.
sentences.spoken: What a lower payment is worth in a bad month, this replay can't measure.

sentences.text: Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect.
sentences.spoken: Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect.

sentences.text: In the 1990s, the typical fallback cost $15,118.
sentences.spoken: In the 1990s, the typical fallback cost fifteen thousand one hundred eighteen dollars.

sentences.text: In the 2000s, with lower rates, it cost about the same: $14,210.
sentences.spoken: In the 2000s, with lower rates, it cost about the same: fourteen thousand two hundred ten dollars.

sentences.text: In the 2010s, rates were far lower, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374.
sentences.spoken: In the 2010s, rates were far lower, yet the fallback cost more: twenty thousand three hundred seventy-four dollars.

sentences.text: The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s.
sentences.spoken: The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about zero point seven point, against about zero point four five in the 1990s and 2000s.

sentences.text: A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one.
sentences.spoken: A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one.

sentences.text: Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack.
sentences.spoken: Since twenty twenty, the typical week priced it at twenty-one thousand three hundred forty-five dollars, close to Tessa's own stack.

sentences.text: That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes.
sentences.spoken: That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes.

sentences.text: Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the 30-year exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day.
sentences.spoken: Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the thirty-year exactly what the fifteen-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day.

sentences.text: At the October eighth rates, it doesn't: it ends about 15 months late.
sentences.spoken: At the October eighth rates, it doesn't: it ends about fifteen months late.

sentences.text: To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment.
sentences.spoken: To finish in fifteen years, she'd add seven hundred thirty-three dollars a month on top of the required payment.

sentences.text: That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner.
sentences.spoken: That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner.

sentences.text: Each extra dollar does cut the next month's interest; the payment just stays fixed, so more of it goes to principal.
sentences.spoken: Each extra dollar does cut the next month's interest; the payment just stays fixed, so more of it goes to principal.

sentences.text: That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong.
sentences.spoken: That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong.

sentences.text: Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month?
sentences.spoken: Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month?

sentences.text: That's one payment a year, the same total as the monthly extra.
sentences.spoken: That's one payment a year, the same total as the monthly extra.

sentences.text: Paid that way, the loan ends four months later.
sentences.spoken: Paid that way, the loan ends four months later.

sentences.text: And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives.
sentences.spoken: And it charges about eight thousand two hundred dollars more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives.

sentences.text: That isn't a verdict on paying yearly: the money stays in her account longer, and what it earns there isn't counted.
sentences.spoken: That isn't a verdict on paying yearly: the money stays in her account longer, and what it earns there isn't counted.

sentences.text: Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn?
sentences.spoken: Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn?

sentences.text: Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate.
sentences.spoken: Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate.

sentences.text: On Tessa's 30-year, that's 7.4 percent a year, before taxes.
sentences.spoken: On Tessa's thirty-year, that's seven point four percent a year, before taxes.

sentences.text: It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays.
sentences.spoken: It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays.

sentences.text: That rate is the bar any other use of that dollar gets measured against, before taxes.
sentences.spoken: That rate is the bar any other use of that dollar gets measured against, before taxes.

sentences.text: How any investment compares, once risk and taxes count, isn't tested here.
sentences.spoken: How any investment compares, once risk and taxes count, isn't tested here.

sentences.text: The bar moves with the rate a loan was taken at.
sentences.spoken: The bar moves with the rate a loan was taken at.

sentences.text: Since 1991, it has stood as high as 9.25 percent.
sentences.spoken: Since nineteen ninety-one, it has stood as high as nine point two five percent.

sentences.text: And as low as 2.65 percent.
sentences.spoken: And as low as two point six five percent.

sentences.text: Only about 1 week in 5 had a bar as high as Tessa's.
sentences.spoken: Only about one week in five had a bar as high as Tessa's.

sentences.text: Leo, also illustrative, took a 30-year loan of the same size in January 2021, the week of that lowest rate, and paid it like a 15-year too.
sentences.spoken: Leo, also illustrative, took a thirty-year loan of the same size in January twenty twenty-one, the week of that lowest rate, and paid it like a fifteen-year too.

sentences.text: His fallback was cheaper: $13,231 over 15 years.
sentences.spoken: His fallback was cheaper: thirteen thousand two hundred thirty-one dollars over fifteen years.

sentences.text: And it left him more room: his required payment sat about $793 a month below the 15-year's.
sentences.spoken: And it left him more room: his required payment sat about seven hundred ninety-three dollars a month below the fifteen-year's.

sentences.text: But his bar was 2.65 percent: each extra dollar he paid earned only that, before taxes.
sentences.spoken: But his bar was two point six five percent: each extra dollar he paid earned only that, before taxes.

sentences.text: [thoughtful] Same plan, a different week, and it means something else.
sentences.spoken: [thoughtful] Same plan, a different week, and it means something else.

sentences.text: For Leo, the stack was short and the bar was low; for Tessa, the stack is tall and the bar is high.
sentences.spoken: For Leo, the stack was short and the bar was low; for Tessa, the stack is tall and the bar is high.

sentences.text: Any fixed-rate borrower can set their own pair beside hers.
sentences.spoken: Any fixed-rate borrower can set their own pair beside hers.

sentences.text: The bar is that loan's own rate, printed on the paperwork, and the stack depends on how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit that week.
sentences.spoken: The bar is that loan's own rate, printed on the paperwork, and the stack depends on how far apart the fifteen-year and thirty-year offers sit that week.

sentences.text: The bar isn't the whole story: a dollar paid into the house is hard to get back in a bad month, which is exactly what the fallback is for.
sentences.spoken: The bar isn't the whole story: a dollar paid into the house is hard to get back in a bad month, which is exactly what the fallback is for.

sentences.text: What this leaves out is on the method card and in the description.
sentences.spoken: What this leaves out is on the method card and in the description.

sentences.text: This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast; it doesn't say which loan to take.
sentences.spoken: This is U.S. only, and it's history, not a forecast; it doesn't say which loan to take.

sentences.text: Beside Tessa's house now stand a tall stack and a high bar.
sentences.spoken: Beside Tessa's house now stand a tall stack and a high bar.

sentences.text: She asked: a 15-year, or a 30-year paid in 15?
sentences.spoken: She asked: a fifteen-year, or a thirty-year paid in fifteen?

sentences.text: [thoughtful] What she now knows: the 30-year paid in 15 is the 15-year plus a fallback, and at the rates of the week of October eighth, 2026, that fallback costs her $120 a month.
sentences.spoken: [thoughtful] What she now knows: the thirty-year paid in fifteen is the fifteen-year plus a fallback, and at the rates of the week of October eighth, twenty twenty-six, that fallback costs her one hundred twenty dollars a month.
